scenes.narration: When you type python greet dot py Asha three, Python stores the words in sys dot argv. It is a list. The first item is the script name, and the rest are your arguments, always as text. For small scripts, that is enough. For bigger ones, the argparse module handles names, types, defaults, and a free help message. Think of a restaurant order. The dish and the extras are given when you order, not after you sit down. In this episode we simulate the command inside the script, so it runs on any computer.

code.source:
import sys

print(sys.argv)
sys.argv = ["greet.py", "Asha", "3"]
name = sys.argv[1]
times = int(sys.argv[2])
for _ in range(times):
    print("Hello", name)

scenes.animation: A typed command splits into word blocks that drop into list slots labelled 0, 1 and 2
scenes.narration: Here is what happens. You type a command. The terminal splits it at the spaces into words. Python stores the words in the list sys dot argv. Index zero is the script name. Index one is the first argument. Index two is the second. All of them are text, even if they look like numbers. So convert with int or float when you need a number.

code.source:
import argparse

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Greet someone")
parser.add_argument("name")
parser.add_argument("--times", type=int, default=1)
args = parser.parse_args(["Asha", "--times", "2"])
for _ in range(args.times):
    print("Hello", args.name)
print(parser.parse_args(["Ravi"]).times)

scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We run the script with no name. The list holds only the script name, so index one does not exist. Index error, list index out of range. Check the length of sys dot argv first, and print a usage line. Better still, use argparse, which checks for you.
